Until now, fixing a code scanning alert meant switching between the alert on github.com and the code in your editor. With the security extension, you can move from finding an alert to fixing it in one place.

Fix the alerts already in your code

If you already run code scanning on your repository, the security extension shows its open code scanning alerts:

  • Browse every open code scanning alert, ordered by severity, and use search and filters to narrow the list.
  • Open an alert to see its details and the affected code. You can open the full alert page on github.com when you need more context.
  • Select one or more alerts and ask Copilot to Explain or Fix them. Copilot only makes fixes in your local working copy and doesn’t commit or push anything. This way you can review and iterate on the changes in the app and push when you’re ready.
  • See linked pull requests on an alert so you know whether someone is already working on a fix.
  • Dismiss alerts you don’t plan to fix. If your organization uses delegated alert dismissal, the extension sends your dismissal for approval.

Catch new issues before you open a pull request
  • Run /security-review on your current changes and see those findings next to your existing alerts.
  • The extension tells you when your code has changed since the last review so you know when to run it again.

You can also ask Copilot about your alerts in chat. Copilot uses the security extension’s tools in the same way as any other tool, following your tool permission settings.

Get started

To install the security extension:

  • In your terminal run copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot.
  • In the GitHub Copilot app, click Customize, search for github-security, then click + Install.

The extension is automatically enabled, and you can open the Security canvas from a session for your repository.

The Explain, Fix, and /security-review actions use the model you’ve selected in the app and consume AI credits in the same way as any other prompt. Browsing and dismissing alerts don’t use AI.

The security extension is in public preview on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported.

  • With any Copilot plan: You can install the extension and run /security-review on your local changes. For Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise, an administrator needs to enable the GitHub Copilot app policy, and can use enterprise managed settings to control which plugins developers can install.
  • With code scanning: You can see, fix, and dismiss existing alerts for repositories where code scanning is enabled and you have permission to view the alerts. Private repositories need GitHub Code Security for this.

Learn more in the security extension documentation and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

The post Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work
items.summary: Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces…
items.html:
Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together. Without that context, agents spend time rediscovering knowledge and can miss your team’s conventions.

GitHub intelligence is the context and learning layer sourced from the graph of GitHub data. It makes this data useful to agents, helping them remember how you work, keep that guidance current, and find the code and development history relevant to the next task. The goal is for agents to build on what you and your team already know, rather than treating every session as a fresh start.

That is the advantage of building where your team’s work already lives. A repository memory can capture why an edge case matters and which test covers it. GitHub intelligence allows agents to use that context, with controls over what they can access.

Three capabilities bring this into your workflow:

  • Memory carries knowledge between sessions
  • Dreaming keeps the context current
  • Code search reaches beyond your checkout.

Availability and settings vary by capability.

Memory: Pick up where you left off

GitHub Copilot Memory is now generally available on paid Copilot plans. Copilot can remember personal preferences and repository conventions across sessions and clients. Memories can be created in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, Slack, Teams, and GitHub Mobile.

You can tell Copilot, Remember to start my pull request descriptions with a TL;DR, and it can reuse that preference across Copilot experiences. Repository memories can capture the right test command or how your team expects Copilot to check its work, so you spend less time repeating guidance in each session. Copilot sessions autonomously generate and curate memories, learning from every interaction.

Among the Copilot CLI sessions reviewed during the public preview where the agent used memory, 93% showed better adherence to developer preferences and 42% showed more efficient workflows attributed to the memories included in the session context.

You can interact with memories in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and VS Code, or manage personal memories in your Copilot settings, where you can view or delete saved preferences.

Dreaming: Continuous context improvement

Copilot dreaming, now in public preview, reflects on past work to improve future agentic sessions.

Three dream types are currently available:

  • Personal memory curation customizes Copilot to your personal preferences by updating memories based on your agent conversations.
  • Repository customization manages repository-scoped memories and proposes updates and improvements to existing skills and custom instruction files.
  • Code review customization turns recurring accepted code-review feedback into guidance for Copilot code review.

Dreaming can add, update, and remove personal and repository memories. Changes to checked-in skills and instructions are proposed in pull requests for your team to review.

Dreaming is opt-in.

  • Individual subscribers: Enable personal curation in your Copilot settings and repository dreams in each repository’s settings. See personal and repository setup.
  • Organizations and enterprises: Administrators enable dreaming through Copilot policies. Enterprise administrators can delegate that choice to organization administrators. Repository dreams cover the repositories allowed by Copilot Memory’s repository access settings. Users must also enable personal dreaming in their own Copilot settings.

Dream runs consume AI credits. See the dreaming documentation for prerequisites, setup, and costs.

Code Search: Reach beyond your checkout

Software projects rarely live in a single repository. GitHub code search helps Copilot find relevant code, configuration, schemas, and documentation across related projects and dependencies without needing a local clone. Copilot can search for exact text and symbols, match patterns with regular expressions, and narrow results by repository, path, or language. Semantic search can also find code by what it does, such as retrying a failed payment, even when you don’t know the file, function name, or repository it lives in.

For example, you’re fixing failed payments, but retry behavior spans a payments service, a shared library, and background workers. Use /research to ask Copilot, How do these components retry failed charges, and where could retries overlap? Copilot can inspect implementations and callers across those repositories to help you understand how the system fits together before changing it.

That unlocks workflows that would otherwise require you to assemble the context yourself:

  • Plan a migration: Use /research to identify implementations and callers across repositories, plan the changes each service needs, and check which projects still use the old API.
  • Investigate a bug: Trace related implementations across services and shared libraries, bring specific code references into the investigation, and use that context to propose a coordinated fix.
  • Follow organizational standards: Find existing patterns across your organization and use them to guide changes in an unfamiliar codebase.

Whether the task calls for an exact symbol, a regular expression in file contents or paths, or a natural-language description, Copilot can search across repositories in your organization to find relevant context. You spend less time cloning projects, tracking down files, and copying code into the conversation. In addition, Copilot gets the context it needs to make the right changes.

Try it today

Your team shouldn’t have to teach every agent the same lessons. GitHub intelligence helps agents carry those lessons forward, find the context they need, and put more of each session toward the work you actually want done.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations
items.summary: Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together. With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously…
items.html:
Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together.

With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously in the cloud, using only the tools you’ve allowed. For example, you could create automations to:

  • Reproduce bugs as soon as an issue is opened.
  • Capture screenshots of the changes when a pull request is marked as ready.
  • Automatically investigate production incidents as soon as they’re detected in your monitoring tool.

Until now, automations have been personal, meaning only you could see and edit them, and they used your identity and AI credits. That works well for automating your own work, like drafting your standup updates, but not for workflows your whole team relies on. Shared automations let your team build and maintain those workflows together.

How shared automations work

  • Visible to your team: Everyone with read access to the repository can see a shared automation, and anyone with write access can edit it.
  • Billed to the repository owner: AI credits are billed to the organization or user that owns the repository, rather than to the person who created the automation.
  • Act as Copilot: Actions on GitHub are attributed to Copilot, rather than to any one user.
  • Built to last: Shared automations belong to the repository, so they keep running if the person who created them leaves the team. Change history lets your team see how the tools, triggers, and prompt have evolved.

For shared automations to run in an organization-owned repository, an administrator must enable the “Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization” policy.

Create a shared automation

When you create an automation on github.com, the GitHub Copilot app , or Visual Studio Code, choose Shared under Type. You can’t change an automation’s type after you create it. To learn more, see personal and shared automations.

Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out to users on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. Availability may vary as the rollout progresses. Once available, you can create automations in any repository where you have write access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Universe releases
items.summary: This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved. Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot…
items.html:
This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved.

Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, start a cloud agent session from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check on it from github.com at lunch. Session continuity lets you pick up the same session across these clients while your agent keeps working in the cloud.

Start and follow cloud sessions across Copilot clients

Hand off work without keeping your computer on. Start a cloud agent session from the Agents window in VS Code. The work runs on GitHub’s infrastructure, so closing your laptop doesn’t stop it.

Find and continue the same session in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Mobile, github.com, or Copilot CLI. Sessions started in a Slack or Microsoft Teams DM can also be continued in these clients.


Keep agents working on your own machines

Move on to another task or project without worrying about losing your session. The new Agent Host isolates your Copilot sessions from individual VS Code windows, so work continues in the background after you close the project folder or window.

You can also run agents on a separate machine while you use your primary development machine for other work. The power and flexibility of VS Code’s Remote SSH and dev tunnels extends to the Agents window. The remote agent works with the same code, tools, and dependencies, and can keep running when you disconnect or quit VS Code locally. The remote machine and its Agent Host must remain running.

Move between the editor and Agents windows

Switch between the editor and the Agents window without starting over. Both views stay in sync with the same live Copilot session.


Control agents on your machine from your phone

Check progress, give direction, or start a new task on your development machine from GitHub Mobile. Your phone provides the controls, and the agent does the work on your development machine. To get started, open a terminal on that machine and run the VS Code CLI command code agent host --github-environment from your project folder. Keep the machine and its Agent Host running while you use it from your phone.


Get a more consistent GitHub Copilot

Get more consistent agent behavior across VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. The Copilot harness, built on the Microsoft Copilot SDK, is now the default for new sessions in both the editor and the Agents window.

Install GitHub Copilot CLI with VS Code

Bring Copilot to your terminal with less setup. Install GitHub Copilot CLI through the VS Code installer on Windows, when adding VS Code to your path on macOS, or by running copilot on Linux.

Compare model results

Explore different approaches to the same coding task. Run models and harnesses in parallel in the Agents window, then review their results side by side. You can ask a Judge model to recommend a solution and choose Synthesize to combine ideas from the other attempts. This is in preview.


Let your agent use your desktop apps

Give your agent tasks that need more than code or terminal commands. With computer use, Copilot can read and interact with desktop apps, including clicking controls and editing text.

On macOS or Windows, open VS Code Settings, search for chat.agentHost.computerUse.enabled, and enable it. Restart VS Code, then run /computer on in a Copilot session running on your computer.

Each application requires your approval. Computer use shares its setup with Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, so on macOS you grant the required system permissions once. Organizations can disable computer use through policy.

This is an experimental feature.


Build your own client

Bring session continuity to your own app. Build a client that connects to an Agent Host and works with the same live sessions as VS Code.

The open Agent Host Protocol (AHP) lets connected clients stay in sync and catch up after reconnecting. Run code agent host, then connect with a client library for TypeScript, Rust, Go, Kotlin, or Swift.

Discover marketplace customizations

Create, discover, and manage agent customizations from one place in VS Code. Open Customizations in the Agents window sidebar or run Chat: Open Customizations. Its “Browse” page brings together skills, MCP servers, plugins, and other customizations from available sources.

The Customization Marketplace is in preview and enabled by default. Business and Enterprise administrators need to allow Editor preview features. Learn more about the Agent Customizations editor and marketplace.

Strengthen existing plugin and marketplace controls

Make existing plugin and marketplace controls more reliable. In VS Code, administrators can use policies to require or block named plugins, add marketplaces, and restrict installation to approved sources. Enterprise-managed strict marketplace settings can also turn off built-in marketplaces. Policy-managed plugin toggles are locked in Customize > Plugins. For controls across Copilot clients, administrators can use enterprise-managed settings.

At the repository level, .github/copilot/settings.json can register plugin marketplaces and enable default plugins. These are defaults, not enforcement: contributors can turn plugins off unless enterprise policy requires them. Learn more about plugin marketplaces and workspace recommendations.

Connect services with Copilot connectors

Bring context from services such as Slack, Notion, and Microsoft Learn into agent sessions without installing or managing an MCP server. Connect once from “Browse” and reuse the connection across supported Copilot clients signed in with the same account.

Connectors are in preview, available on all Copilot plans, and work with the Copilot harness. Business and Enterprise administrators need to allow Editor preview features. Learn more about Copilot connectors in VS Code.

Learn more

Learn more in the VS Code release notes

items.title: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls generally available
items.summary: Repository plugin defaults and enterprise-managed plugin controls are now generally available in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Trusted repositories can install and enable default plugins for contributors. Enterprises can require plugins,…
items.html:
Repository plugin defaults and enterprise-managed plugin controls are now generally available in VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. Trusted repositories can install and enable default plugins for contributors. Enterprises can require plugins, block plugins, and restrict installation to approved marketplaces.

As a repository maintainer, you can define a plugin marketplace and default plugins so contributors don’t have to repeat setup for each project. Contributors can turn off repository defaults where policy permits.

As an enterprise administrator, you can supply approved marketplaces and require or block plugins through managed settings. Required plugins are automatically installed and enabled, and users can’t disable them. Managed settings take precedence over repository and personal choices.

Repository defaults are available to individual Copilot users and users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise.

Managed controls are available on GitHub Enterprise Cloud for users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise licenses issued by the enterprise or one of its organizations.

Learn more about plugins for GitHub Copilot.

The post Repository plugin defaults and enterprise plugin controls generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Generate and edit images directly in Copilot
items.summary: You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your…
items.html:
You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project.

Previously, getting a visual asset while working in Copilot meant stepping away to a separate tool, describing what you needed again, generating it there, and manually bringing it back into your project. This update removes that context switch, so you can go from an idea to a usable image without breaking your flow.

  • Describe an image conversationally in any Copilot chat session, whether you’re starting a new request or in the middle of a coding task.
  • Copilot previews the generated image inline and saves it directly to your workspace.
  • Organization and enterprise owners can turn off image generation by disabling the image generation model using Copilot model policies.
  • You can opt in to a visible “Made with AI” watermark on images Copilot generates and edits. Watermarking is off by default.

To try it, open a Copilot chat in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI and describe the image you want.

Image generation is in public preview for Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise. It’s billed separately from your chat model, based on image tokens that count toward your plan’s AI credits.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post Generate and edit images directly in Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.html:
• Added support for all GPT-5 models.

  • Added support for Grok-4 via xai/grok-4 and openrouter/x-ai/grok-4 model names.

  • Added support for gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-lite-preview-06-17 model, by Tamir Zahavi-Brunner.

  • /clear now prints “All chat history cleared.” so you know it worked, by Zexin Yuan.

  • /undo output now shows only the first line of each commit message, making it easier to read.

  • Added support for openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k2 model, by Jack Harrington.

  • Display model announcements with no-arg /model command.

  • Fixed an issue where new settings for an existing model didn't replace the old ones, by Andrew Grigorev.

  • Fixed analytics to support the latest PostHog SDK event-capture API.

  • Bumped dependencies to pick up latest litellm==1.75.0.

  • Aider wrote 88% of the code in this release.

items.title: Aider v0.85.0
items.summary: New Models Added support for new Gemini models including gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, and gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 with thinking tokens support. Updated model aliases: flash now points to gemini-2.5-flash and gemini now points to gemini-2.5-pro.…
items.html:
New Models

  • Added support for new Gemini models including gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, and gemini-2.5-pro-preview-06-05 with thinking tokens support.
  • Updated model aliases: flash now points to gemini-2.5-flash and gemini now points to gemini-2.5-pro.
  • Support for Responses API models like o1-pro, o3-pro.
  • Added support for OpenAI o3-pro model across multiple providers.
  • Enhanced thinking tokens support: can now be disabled by setting to 0, and improved help text with examples.
  • Increased max tokens for Deepseek models to 65536 for better performance.
  • Updated pricing for o3.

New Features & Enhancements

  • Added --add-gitignore-files flag to enable adding files listed in .gitignore to Aider's editing scope, by omarcinkonis.
  • Co-authored-by attribution is now enabled by default for commit messages.
  • Enhanced commit message generation to use system prompt prefixes, by Luke Reeves.
  • Added --commit-language option to specify the language for commit messages, by Kyosuke Takayama.
  • Skip expensive file tracking operations when --skip-sanity-check-repo is enabled for better performance, by Makar Ivashko.
  • Optimized chat history summarization performance, by jayeshthk.
  • Added custom PostHog analytics configuration options with --analytics-posthog-host and --analytics-posthog-project-api-key flags, by Vasil Markoukin.

Repository Map

  • Added MATLAB language support for repository maps, by Matthew Tofano.
  • Added Clojure language support for repository maps, by Garrett Hopper.
  • Improved kebab-case identifier recognition in repository maps for better code analysis.

Fixes & Small Improvements

  • Improved GitHub Copilot token handling with better validation and error messages, by Vincent Taverna and Sebastian Estrella.

  • Improved inline code rendering in Rich markdown output, by Vamsi Talupula.

  • Fixed Vertex AI model name prefixes in settings, by Wietse Venema.

  • Improved /read-only command to resolve literal paths correctly, by Matteo Landi.

  • Fixed encoding issues in git diff output and LLM history logging.

  • Fixed search block regex to accept optional closing tags when working with HTML content, by Mathis Beer.

  • Auto-create parent directories for chat history files to prevent startup errors, by contributor.

  • Ensure pip is available before package installation.

  • Aider wrote 21% of the code in this release.

Model support & provider updates

  • Added support for new Claude models including the Sonnet 4 and Opus 4 series (e.g., claude-sonnet-4-20250514, claude-opus-4-20250514) across various providers. The default sonnet and opus aliases were updated to these newer versions.

Core functionality improvements

  • Fixed OpenRouter token cost calculation for improved accuracy.

Quality of life improvements

  • Improved OpenRouter model metadata handling by introducing a local cache, increasing reliability and performance.
  • Added shell tab completion for file path arguments (by saviour) and for --edit-format/--editor-edit-format options.
  • The /settings command now displays detailed metadata for active main, editor, and weak models.
  • Improved user language detection by correctly normalizing hyphenated language codes (e.g., en-US to en) and enhancing the validation of locale results.
  • Prevented aider from instructing the LLM to reply in 'C' or 'POSIX' when these are detected as the system locale.
  • Displayed a spinner with the model name when generating commit messages.
  • Bumped configargparse to 1.7.1 as 1.7 was pulled.

  • Added support for qwen3-235b models.
  • Added repo-map support for OCaml and OCaml interface files, by Andrey Popp.
  • Added a spinner animation while waiting for the LLM to start streaming its response.
  • Updated the spinner animation to a Knight Rider style.
  • Introduced --attribute-co-authored-by option to add co-author trailer to commit messages, by Andrew Grigorev.
  • Updated Gemini model aliases (e.g., gemini, gemini-2.5-pro) to point to the 05-06 preview versions.
  • Marked Gemini 2.5 Pro preview models as overeager by default.
  • Commit message prompt specifies the user's language.
  • Updated the default weak model for Gemini 2.5 Pro models to gemini/gemini-2.5-flash-preview-04-17.
  • Corrected gemini-2.5-pro-exp-03-25 model settings to reflect its lack of support for thinking_budget.
  • Ensured model-specific system prompt prefixes are placed on a new line before the main system prompt.
  • Added tracking of total tokens sent and received, now included in benchmark statistics.
  • Automatically fetch model parameters (context window, pricing) for OpenRouter models directly from their website, by Stefan Hladnik.
  • Enabled support for thinking_tokens and reasoning_effort parameters for OpenRouter models.
  • Improved cost calculation using litellm.completion_cost where available.
  • Added model settings for openrouter/google/gemini-2.5-pro-preview-03-25.
  • Added --disable-playwright flag to prevent Playwright installation prompts and usage, by Andrew Grigorev.
  • The aider scrape command-line tool will now use Playwright for web scraping if it is available, by Jon Keys.
  • Fixed linter command execution on Windows by adopting oslex for argument quoting, by Titusz Pan.
  • Improved cross-platform display of shell commands by using oslex for robust argument quoting, by Titusz Pan.
  • Improved /ask mode to instruct the LLM to elide unchanging code in its responses.
  • Ensured web scraping in the GUI also respects Playwright availability and the --disable-playwright flag.
  • Improved display of filenames in the prompt header using rich Text formatting.
  • Enabled reasoning_effort for Gemini 2.5 Flash models.
  • Added a --shell-completions argument to generate shell completion scripts (e.g., for bash, zsh).
  • Explicit --attribute-author or --attribute-committer flags now override the default behavior when --attribute-co-authored-by is used, allowing finer control over commit attribution, by Andrew Grigorev.
  • Fixed an issue where read-only status of files might not be preserved correctly by some commands (e.g. /drop after adding a read-only file).
  • The aider-args utility (or python -m aider.args) now defaults to printing a sample YAML configuration if no arguments are provided.
  • Displayed token count progress and the name of the file or identifier being processed during repo map updates.
  • Extended the waiting spinner to also show for non-streaming responses and further enhanced its animation with console width clipping, cursor hiding, and a more continuous appearance.
  • Dropped support for Python 3.9.

items.html:
What's Changed

  • fix(listener): bound startup after the 0.34.17 heartbeat regression by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5168
  • fix(listener): decouple channel gateway startup from connection readiness by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5208
  • fix(listener): keep the runtime across re-registration by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5207
  • fix(recovery): don't tell the model to blindly re-issue stale tool calls by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5173
  • fix(listener): retry listener-state renames on Windows by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5120
  • fix(listener): time out git context refresh and log close reasons by @cpacker in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5037
  • fix(tui): stop stale approval recovery from denying already-resolved calls by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5236
  • fix(listener): back off and stop recovery retries on owner_mismatch by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5151
  • fix: let CLI subcommands drain before exiting on Windows by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5171
  • fix(updater): don't kill an in-progress global install by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5164
  • fix(listener): treat a pre-reboot listener lock as stale by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5205
  • fix(cron): reclaim pre-reboot scheduler lease held by a reused non-letta pid by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5216
  • fix(permissions): check allowed directories on path boundaries, not string prefixes by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5189
  • fix(approval): don't treat schema-allowed null as a missing required arg by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5186
  • fix(local): report step_count for each completed local step by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5187
  • fix(local): scope active runs by agent and conversation by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5188
  • fix(listener): enforce max_turns when a turn stops for approval by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5190
  • fix(windows): detect pwsh installed as an MSIX app execution alias by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5165
  • fix(channels): apply the Discord account's permission mode to its turns by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5139
  • fix(channels): don't swallow a message after a stale approval prompt by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5130
  • fix: log cron prompt delivery on listener dequeue by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5241
  • docs(cron): device-pinned schedules fail when the computer is offline, no cloud fallback by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5238
  • test: expect nextCursor in computers list exit test (fix main after #5213) by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5246
  • fix: patch Node runtimes for CVE-2026-111497 by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5222
  • fix(local): don't cap replayed tool_call_id at 40 for OpenAI-compatible proxies by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5185
  • fix(listener): don't render the spinner UI when stdout isn't a TTY by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5253
  • fix(listener): send queued inputs with the next model request again [LET-14221] by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5254
  • chore(queue): remove unused approval_result and overlay_action queue kinds by @letta-integration[bot] in https://github.com/letta-ai/letta-code/pull/5255

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 28, 2026
items.summary: Get an email before your credits run out Workspace admins and owners now get an email when your credits are likely to run out before your monthly credits refill. The email shows the expected run-out date and the refill date, so you can add credits before the…
items.html:
Get an email before your credits run out

Workspace admins and owners now get an email when your credits are likely to run out before your monthly credits refill. The email shows the expected run-out date and the refill date, so you can add credits before the run-out date. Lovable bases the estimate on your workspace's recent Run credits usage, so credits you spend building are not part of it. Lovable sends no email while auto top-up is enabled and not paused.

Redesigned Share menu

The Share menu in your project has a simpler layout. The Workspace access row sets what the rest of your workspace can do with the project. The invite link has one setting for its access level, with Copy next to it. Preview links are listed by name, and you edit or delete a link from its row.

Set up two-factor authentication from the dashboard banner

The banner on your dashboard now opens the two-factor authentication setup dialog directly. Lovable shows the banner if you log in with email and password and have not set up two-factor authentication. In the dialog, choose an authenticator app or your phone.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 27, 2026
items.summary: Events & hooks for your workspace Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans can now extend their workspace with their own services using Events & Hooks. Events notify your HTTPS endpoint when a project is created, published, transferred to…
items.html:
Events & hooks for your workspace

Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans can now extend their workspace with their own services using Events & Hooks. Events notify your HTTPS endpoint when a project is created, published, transferred to another workspace, or deleted. Hooks let your endpoint allow or block an action first, such as checking a message sent in a project's chat for sensitive data before Lovable processes it. Find it in your workspace settings.

Connect your app to Scrive

You can now connect your Lovable app to Scrive for e-signatures and electronic identification (eID). Scrive eSign sends documents for signature and tracks their signing status. Scrive eID Hub verifies who your app's users are with national eIDs such as BankID and MitID. It fits contract sending portals, onboarding with signed agreements, and identity-verified sign-ups. Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

Redesigned sidebar

The sidebar now organizes your projects and chats into three sections: Pinned, Projects, and Recent chats. Pinned replaces Starred and shows the projects and chats you pinned, with the most recently pinned first. Projects and Recent chats each link to their full list.

Knowledge is now Instructions

In workspace and project settings, Knowledge is now Instructions. Workspace knowledge and project knowledge are now called workspace instructions and project instructions. They work the same way, so nothing changes for your projects.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 26, 2026
items.summary: Manage IdP group mappings in one place Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans now map IdP groups to workspace roles in the Provisioning groups section of the workspace's Identity settings. On Enterprise plans, SCIM provisioning uses the…
items.html:
Manage IdP group mappings in one place

Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans now map IdP groups to workspace roles in the Provisioning groups section of the workspace's Identity settings. On Enterprise plans, SCIM provisioning uses the same mappings. Workspace owners can also map a group to the Owner role.

Redesigned connector pages

Each connector's page now has a Connect button that creates the first connection type the connector supports. More options lists the other types. The connector's connections appear in one Connections list, where the Visibility column shows whether each one is Private or Shared. You can sort the list by name, visibility, or number of projects.

Scroll through all files in the Files tab

Your project's Files tab now loads more files as you scroll, so you can browse a large project's files in one list.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 22, 2026
items.summary: Clearer Privacy & security settings The Privacy & security settings have reworded labels and descriptions that say what each setting controls. Changes with a wide effect, such as enabling automatic deletion of abandoned projects or restricting code downloads,…
items.html:
Clearer Privacy & security settings

The Privacy & security settings have reworded labels and descriptions that say what each setting controls. Changes with a wide effect, such as enabling automatic deletion of abandoned projects or restricting code downloads, now open a confirmation dialog that shows what the change does. The change applies after you confirm. Three settings have new names: Default website access is now Default published app access, External invites is now External viewer invites, and the Security automation section is now Security checks.

Folder access applies to personal folders only

When a personal folder becomes a workspace folder, the access levels you granted stop applying to the projects inside it. The people and groups you invited keep their workspace role and any access you gave them on a project directly.

Gemini 2.5 chat models are retired for your app's AI features

The Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite chat models (google/gemini-2.5-pro, google/gemini-2.5-flash, and google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite) are no longer available for your app's AI features. They retired on October 20, 2026. Your app's requests for Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash now go to Gemini 3.8 Flash, and requests for Flash Lite go to Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite. Your app keeps working without a code change, but the replacement can cost a different amount per request and respond differently. If your app uses one of these models, ask Lovable to switch it to a current model.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 21, 2026
items.summary: See adoption by department without SCIM Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans can now see adoption by department in Insights when your workspace uses SSO without SCIM. To set it up, map the department attribute in your SAML or OIDC app.…
items.html:
See adoption by department without SCIM

Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans can now see adoption by department in Insights when your workspace uses SSO without SCIM. To set it up, map the department attribute in your SAML or OIDC app. Lovable then reads it at each sign-in, so the breakdown fills as your members return.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 20, 2026
items.summary: Group your workspaces into an organization Enterprise companies that run several Lovable workspaces can now manage them together in an organization. The company sets up SSO once for all of them, and with SCIM the identity provider adds and removes members…
items.html:
Group your workspaces into an organization

Enterprise companies that run several Lovable workspaces can now manage them together in an organization. The company sets up SSO once for all of them, and with SCIM the identity provider adds and removes members automatically. Org admins see every member and role in one place, and teams can publish internal apps to everyone in the company. Each workspace keeps its own projects, members, groups, and billing. Lovable sets this up on request through your account team.

Let Lovable create your Supabase project

You can now ask Lovable to create a Supabase project for an app that has no backend. You choose the organization and the region, and Lovable creates the project there and connects it to your app. This works in workspaces where the built-in backend is disabled. A project's region cannot be changed later, and Supabase bills the new project to your own organization.

App + chat connectors: LlamaParse Platform and n8n

LlamaParse Platform lets apps parse documents and extract structured data from them, such as the parties and dates in a contract. Use it for document review tools, knowledge base assistants, and apps that read the files your users upload. With Managed by Lovable, parsing and extraction spend workspace credits.

n8n lets apps list workflows, read executions, trigger webhooks, and publish or unpublish workflows on your n8n instance. Use it for internal consoles, intake forms, and status pages built on workflows you already run.

Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

Seedream 5 Pro and Seedance 2.5 for your app's AI features

Your app's AI features can now use two new ByteDance models:

  • Seedream 5 Pro (bytedance/seedream-5-pro) generates and edits images from a text prompt and up to 10 reference images, for posters, ads, and designs. It renders text inside the image accurately.
  • Seedance 2.5 (bytedance/seedance-2.5) generates 4 to 30 second video clips with synchronized sound, at 480p or 720p. It takes reference images, video, and audio, and can edit and extend an existing clip.

Workspace admins and owners enable ByteDance in Connectors first. Ask Lovable to use either model in your app.

Redesigned More menu

The More menu now lists your project's services directly in the sidebar: Database, Users, Storage, Emails, and Usage. Agent integrations is grouped under AI, and Secrets under Settings. The SQL editor, Edge functions, and Jobs are in the Database view, under Manage.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 19, 2026
items.summary: Connect your app to Cube You can now connect your Lovable app to Cube to read the measures and dimensions your data team defines in its semantic layer, on Cube Cloud or on a Cube Core instance you host yourself. It fits dashboards, reports, and internal tools…
items.html:
Connect your app to Cube

You can now connect your Lovable app to Cube to read the measures and dimensions your data team defines in its semantic layer, on Cube Cloud or on a Cube Core instance you host yourself. It fits dashboards, reports, and internal tools built on the metrics your company already agrees on. The connection is read-only. Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

Faster dictation

Dictation now transcribes while you speak, so your text is ready when you stop recording. It works in the project chat, in Chats, on the create form, and in the mobile apps.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 18, 2026
items.summary: Request edit access to a project you can only view You can now ask for edit access without leaving the project. Select Request to edit at the top of the project and add an optional message. Lovable emails the project's owner, or the workspace's admins and…
items.html:
Request edit access to a project you can only view

You can now ask for edit access without leaving the project. Select Request to edit at the top of the project and add an optional message. Lovable emails the project's owner, or the workspace's admins and owners, who can approve or deny the request.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 17, 2026
items.summary: Request a higher workspace role Workspace viewers and editors can now request a higher role from the People tab. Viewers can ask for editor or admin access, and editors for admin access, each with an optional reason. You can withdraw a request while it is…
items.html:
Request a higher workspace role

Workspace viewers and editors can now request a higher role from the People tab. Viewers can ask for editor or admin access, and editors for admin access, each with an optional reason. You can withdraw a request while it is pending. Workspace admins and owners approve or deny it. Admin access requires a paid workspace plan.

Jump to your last chat in the desktop app

In the Lovable desktop app, tap Ctrl+Tab to switch to the chat you were in before. Hold Ctrl and press Tab to pick from your recent chats instead, with the chat you are in first. The shortcut uses Ctrl on macOS as well.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 16, 2026
items.summary: Require approval or block publishing with workspace policies Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now set workspace policies that block publishing or require an admin or owner to approve it first. Policies cover apps with unresolved findings of…
items.html:
Require approval or block publishing with workspace policies

Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now set workspace policies that block publishing or require an admin or owner to approve it first. Policies cover apps with unresolved findings of personal data, apps published by external collaborators, apps published publicly, apps that use connectors, and publishing from unverified email domains. When a policy requires approval, the person publishing sends a request from the publish dialog, and Lovable publishes the app when an admin or owner approves it. Enable policies in your workspace's Privacy & security settings.

Review publish requests and findings in the Action center

Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans now have an Action center in the dashboard sidebar. It lists what needs a decision: publish requests waiting for approval, projects whose owner left the workspace, projects whose credit usage rose sharply, public apps with critical security findings, and public apps with no edits for months. From each row you can approve or deny a request, assign an owner, or unpublish an app.

Add OIDC sign-in to your app

In an app on the built-in backend (Cloud), you can now let your users sign in with your own OpenID Connect provider, such as Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Keycloak, next to the other sign-in methods. Enable OIDC in your project's authentication settings and enter the details from your provider. Lovable then starts a build that adds the sign-in button to your app. The build is treated as standard build usage and consumes credits. Sign-ins consume no credits.

Lovable writes and runs tests for the rules you change

Lovable now adds a small test when you add or change a rule in your app, such as a price, a limit, or a permission. It runs the tests that cover the change before it reports the work as done, and keeps the tests in your project. Lovable does not write tests for copy, styling, or markup.

Connect your app to Pledge

You can now connect your Lovable app to Pledge to search verified nonprofits worldwide, create and track donations, and create and update fundraisers. It fits donation checkouts, loyalty point redemption, cause campaign pages, and employee giving programs. Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

GPT Transcribe for your app's speech-to-text features

Your app's AI features can now use OpenAI's GPT Transcribe (openai/gpt-transcribe), the new default speech-to-text model. It accepts audio files up to 25 MB, and your app can pass context, expected keywords, and languages as hints for names and specialist vocabulary. Ask Lovable to use it in your app, or describe what you want and let Lovable pick.

Formatted Markdown previews in the Files tab

Markdown files in your project's Files tab now open as formatted text, with tables, task lists, footnotes, and code blocks you can copy. Markdown files in Chats open in the same preview.

Larger document previews in the Files tab

A document you open in your project's Files tab now fills the preview pane. Its actions, such as adding it to the chat or a collection, are in the header above the document.

Removed: tabs in the desktop app

Tabs have been removed from the Lovable desktop app in version 1.9. The sidebar already lists your chats and projects, so the tabs were redundant. Switch between chats and projects from the sidebar, or hold Ctrl+Tab to pick from your recent chats. New downloads include 1.9, and the app offers the update when you open it.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 15, 2026
items.summary: Export audit logs to your SIEM or cloud storage Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now schedule exports of the workspace's audit logs to Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, Splunk, or Azure Log Analytics. Lovable delivers new…
items.html:
Export audit logs to your SIEM or cloud storage

Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now schedule exports of the workspace's audit logs to Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, Splunk, or Azure Log Analytics. Lovable delivers new events every hour or every 3 hours, so you can keep an audit trail for longer than the 13 weeks Lovable stores it and search Lovable activity next to your other security events. Find it under Workspace settings → Security → Data exports. Data exports come at no extra charge from Lovable. Your destination provider bills you for storage and ingestion.

Use Lovable from Claude through your company's SSO

Workspace admins and owners on Business and Enterprise plans can now enable enterprise-managed authentication, so members use the Lovable MCP server in Claude with their Okta identity, without a separate Lovable sign-in. Enable it in your workspace's Identity settings and pick the SSO provider your team already uses. Members keep their existing workspace and project permissions. Claude requires a Team or Enterprise plan.

Login pages include Sign in with Lovable by default

Login pages that Lovable builds for an app with Lovable Cloud now include Sign in with Lovable by default, alongside email and password sign-in and Google sign-in. Your app's users can sign in with their Lovable account, and Lovable registers the sign-in for your project with nothing to configure. To use a different set of methods, name them in your prompt. Sign-ins consume no credits.

GPT-6.1 Sol for your app's AI features

Your app's AI features can now use OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol (openai/gpt-6.1-sol), a model for complex coding and professional work. It accepts text and image input and responds with text. Ask Lovable to use it in your app, or describe what you want and let Lovable pick.

Documents in the project chat show their name and type

Documents that Lovable creates or refers to in a project chat reply now appear as a list with each file's name and a file-type icon, separate from the preview grid for images and videos. A single document with a preview, such as a PDF or a Markdown file, appears as a larger preview card. Select a row or card to open the file in the Files tab.

Select and sort files faster in the Files tab

In your project's Files tab, you can now select several files by hovering over a file and selecting its checkbox, then add them to the chat or a collection, download them, or delete them. Inside a collection, you can now sort files by Updated, Name, or Size, and the sort button shows which field is active. In list view, each document shows a file-type icon.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 14, 2026
items.summary: Growth tools: from building your app to growing it Lovable now helps you find customers, from the same chat where you build. Set a goal such as "my first 100 signups", and Growth tools turn it into a plan built from your app, your audience, and your traffic.…
items.html:
Growth tools: from building your app to growing it

Lovable now helps you find customers, from the same chat where you build. Set a goal such as "my first 100 signups", and Growth tools turn it into a plan built from your app, your audience, and your traffic. Lovable tells you what to fix first, and says so when ads are premature.

  • Growth advice that knows your app. Lovable recommends your next move: help search engines and AI assistants find your app, sharpen the offer on your landing page, prepare posts and listings for the communities, directories, and creators that reach your audience, or set up a Google Business Profile for a local business.
  • Ads launched from Lovable. Create a new Google Ads account or connect an existing one, and use your Facebook account for ads on Facebook and Instagram. Lovable sets up tracking and creates campaigns on Google, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram. You decide the ad budget and approve when spending can start.
  • Creative built from your app. Ask for a launch video, an animated product demo, a video ad, images, or ad copy that match your brand, ready for a campaign, a social post, or customer outreach.

Results show in the redesigned Analytics view: visits by channel, campaign results on the Ads tab, and a Get more visitors button that sends your current traffic to Lovable with your request. Lovable adds no extra fees for using Growth tools, and the standard costs of chatting with Lovable apply. Google or Meta charges the payment method on your advertising account for the ads you run.

Add Sign in with Lovable to any website

You can now let people sign in to your website with their Lovable account, including a site you did not build with Lovable. Add one script tag and a button, and your site receives the person's name, email address, and picture, depending on which of those you ask for. If your site has a server, you can use the standard OpenID Connect flow in place of the script. Both paths start from an OAuth client registered in your workspace settings. Sign-ins consume no credits.

Connect your apps to Lovable with OAuth

Workspace admins and owners can now register OAuth clients under Workspace settings → API keys & OAuth → OAuth clients. An OAuth client lets your app ask each user to allow access to their profile, projects, or workspaces, and gives you a client ID and, for a Web server client, a client secret. Sensitive scopes, which read or change projects and workspaces, require a Business or Enterprise plan and verification from Lovable. Users see a warning until the client is verified.

Let your app's users sign in with their Lovable account

In an app with Lovable Cloud, you can now let your users sign in with their Lovable account. Enable it in your project's auth settings, or ask Lovable in the project chat to add the button. Lovable registers the sign-in for your project and keeps it current when your app's address changes. Your app receives each user's name, email address, and profile picture, and the consent screen shows your project's name. Sign-ins consume no credits.

Ask Lovable what drives your run credit usage

You can now ask Lovable what drives run credit usage in the project chat. Lovable reads the recorded usage, investigates the app's scheduled jobs, functions, database, storage, and AI activity, traces what it finds to the project's code, and proposes fixes. Lovable makes a change only when you ask for it. Workspace admins and owners can also ask in Chats which projects and usage categories drive the whole workspace's run credit usage.

From the usage chart, workspace admins and owners can start the same investigation with Optimize your usage. The button appears below the chart in Usage details and in a project's Cloud usage view when the workspace or project used more than 5 run credits in the last 7 days. In Usage details, it starts a workspace-wide investigation in Chats. In a project, it starts the investigation in the project chat, in Chat mode, where Lovable does not edit your project's code.

Connect your app to Bing Webmaster Tools

You can now connect your Lovable app to Bing Webmaster Tools to read clicks, impressions, top queries, and crawl stats for the sites verified in your Bing Webmaster Tools account, and to submit URLs and sitemaps. It fits search dashboards, crawl monitors, and tools that send new pages or feeds to Bing. Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

Restore a deleted project yourself

You can now restore a deleted project for 60 days after you delete it. Select Restore under Recently deleted projects in your workspace settings. The project returns with its code, version history, and chat history, and a paused Cloud backend resumes. You can restore the projects you own. Workspace owners can restore every deleted project in the workspace, whoever deleted it. After 60 days, the project is permanently deleted.

Restore a deleted workspace yourself

Workspace owners on Free, Pro, and Business plans can now restore a deleted workspace, with its projects and members, for 60 days after deleting it. Select Restore under Recently deleted workspaces in your account settings. If the workspace's subscription ended while it was deleted, the workspace returns on the Free plan. After 60 days, the workspace is permanently deleted.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 13, 2026
items.summary: Let browser agents use your app You can now let browser agents use your app. When you enable agent integrations, Lovable also adds WebMCP tools to your app, so an AI agent built into the browser can act on the page a person has open, such as marking a task as…
items.html:
Let browser agents use your app

You can now let browser agents use your app. When you enable agent integrations, Lovable also adds WebMCP tools to your app, so an AI agent built into the browser can act on the page a person has open, such as marking a task as done or filtering a list. Browser tools run in the person's own browser tab with their signed-in session, separate from your app's MCP server, and you can also ask Lovable in the project chat to add them without a server. Lovable starts with tools that read information or are easy to undo, and adds tools that delete, pay, send, publish, or share only when you ask.

Gemini 4 Argon for your app's AI features

Your app's AI features can now use Google's Gemini 4 Argon (google/gemini-4-argon), a frontier model for long-horizon coding, reasoning, and knowledge work. It accepts text, image, audio, and video input and comes at a premium price. Ask Lovable to use it in your app, or describe what you want and let Lovable pick.

Approve every tool from a chat connector at once

You can now select Always allow all tools from this connection when Lovable asks you to approve a tool from a chat connector, and every tool from that connection runs without asking from then on, including tools the server adds later. The choice applies to your own approvals only, and you can change it in the connection's settings in Connectors.

Supported PostgreSQL extensions on Lovable Cloud

Lovable Cloud databases support a fixed set of PostgreSQL extensions, such as pg_cron, pg_net, vector, and postgis. Lovable now refuses CREATE EXTENSION for any other extension, in the project chat, the SQL editor, and the Lovable API, and builds the feature with plain SQL instead. Extensions already installed in your database keep working.

Search for individual settings

You can now search for individual settings in workspace settings. Start typing in the search box at the top of the settings sidebar, and the results list the matching settings grouped by settings page, with the matching words highlighted. Select a result to open that setting.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 12, 2026
items.summary: Edit images directly in the Files tab You can now mark a change directly on an image in your project's Files tab. Open the image and select Edit, then draw over an area and describe the change, pin a comment where you want something changed, erase what you…
items.html:
Edit images directly in the Files tab

You can now mark a change directly on an image in your project's Files tab. Open the image and select Edit, then draw over an area and describe the change, pin a comment where you want something changed, erase what you want removed, or remove the background. Lovable saves the result as a new file next to the original.

See how much usage your free allowances cover

On Free, Pro, and Business plans, you can now see how much of your usage the free allowances covered. Usage details shows the covered credits next to the total above the chart, and the By coverage view splits each bar into what the daily build credits, the daily chat allowance, and the monthly Cloud, AI, and connector grants paid for, and what drew on your general credits.

Connect your app to Loops

You can now connect your Lovable app to Loops to create and update contacts, send events that start your Loops automations, and send transactional email you manage in Loops. It fits waitlists, signup forms, and product notifications that should reach people from your Loops audience. Add it from Connectors, or ask Lovable in a project to connect it.

items.title: Lovable changelog — Oct 9, 2026
items.summary: Publish every app in your workspace under your own domain Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now set a publishing domain for the workspace, so projects publish at your-app.yourdomain.com instead of your-app.lovable.app. Pick a domain you…
items.html:
Publish every app in your workspace under your own domain

Workspace admins and owners on Enterprise plans can now set a publishing domain for the workspace, so projects publish at your-app.yourdomain.com instead of your-app.lovable.app. Pick a domain you bought through Lovable, or a subdomain of it, with no DNS setup. You can also connect a domain or subdomain you own elsewhere. Each project moves to the new address the next time you publish it, and its existing lovable.app address keeps working. Find it under Workspace settings → Workspace domains → Publishing domain.

Reference another chat or send it a task

In Chats, you can now work with your other chats. Reference a chat to let Lovable read what you discussed there, or ask Lovable to send a message to another chat or to start a new chat with a first task. Type @ and select the chat under Chats, or paste a link to the chat. The other chat does the work and can reply in your conversation, so one chat can coordinate several others.

Generate a secret that another app also needs

When Lovable asks you for a secret that you enter in two places, such as the secret GitHub uses to sign its webhook requests or a token two of your apps share, the secret form now has a Generate button. Select it to fill in a strong random value, copy the value to the other place, and submit. Lovable shows the value only in the form, and does not repeat stored secret values, or anything derived from them, in the project chat, in logs, or in your code.

Buy .si domains through Lovable

You can now buy .si domains, the Slovenian country-code extension, through Lovable. Search for the full name including the extension from Buy a domain in your project's or workspace's domain settings. A new .si domain can take up to 2 hours to start working, and you can register it for up to 5 years.

Get a warning before your credits run out

On Free, Pro, and Business plans, workspace admins and owners now get a warning when the workspace is likely to run out of credits before its monthly credits refill. The warning appears on the Plans & credit usage page and in Usage details, shows when your credits are expected to run out and when your monthly credits refill, and lets you add credits before your published apps are affected.

Enterprise credit balances now appear as numbers

On Enterprise plans, the credit panel on the Plans & credit usage page now shows your balance as numbers in place of a progress bar. Admins and owners see how many workspace credits remain and the workspace total, for example 6,400 remaining of 10,000. When the workspace has used more than its commitment, they also see a warning and an Overage credits row. Other members see only their own personal credits.
